store_data.about_the_game:
BUILD THE COMIC SHOP OF YOUR DREAMS

Comic Shop Tycoon is a first person shop management simulator where you start with a small comic book store and work to turn it into a successful business.

Order new inventory, unpack deliveries, stock your shelves, set your prices, ring up customers, and put your profits back into the store. Each day gives you another chance to improve the shop, bring in more products, and grow your business.

RUN YOUR SHOP YOUR WAY

You take care of the day to day work yourself. Keep your shelves stocked, clean up the store, manage incoming deliveries, work the register, and make sure your customers can find something they want to buy.

STOCK MORE THAN COMICS

As your store grows, so does the selection of products you can sell. Along with comic books, you can carry collectibles, figures, tabletop RPG books, dice, comic supplies, and other merchandise.

KEEP UP WITH NEW RELEASES

New comics arrive over time, so you will need to plan ahead, order what you need, and make room on your shelves. Keeping popular products in stock can make a big difference when customers come through the door.

GROW YOUR BUSINESS

Earn money and experience by running the store. Unlock new products, expand your available space, improve your shop, and keep working toward something bigger.

MAKE THE STORE YOURS

Decorate and customize your comic shop with posters, standees, fixtures, murals, and other items. Build a store that feels like your own and give customers a place they will want to come back to.

BUILD YOUR COMIC SHOP EMPIRE

Start small, learn the business, and build your store into the kind of comic shop you would want to visit yourself.

store_data.about_the_game:
Your power is in the cards you can't draw.

Every creature card belongs to a strain. Play one and it doesn't hit for the number printed on it — it hits for the entire population of that strain, everywhere in your deck at once. Draw pile, discard, hand, all of it counts. You never need to find the right card. You only need it to exist.

Every card asks the same question, every turn.

HARVEST it for damage now, or SOW it to breed more of its strain and hit harder for the rest of the run. There is no energy bar. Your hand refills to five and every card in it is yours to spend — the cost of sowing is simply the damage you chose not to deal. Greed has an axis: go deep on one strain for a multiplier that collapses all at once, or go wide for something steady that never spikes.

Carrying capacity is the ceiling. Going over it is how you get ammunition.

Every strain has its own cap. Cross it and breeding stalls, the end of each turn spits Feral cards into your deck, and if two strains are over at once the larger one eats the smaller. Feral cards are dead weight you cannot play. They are also the only fuel for BLOOM.

BLOOM is a bomb you build out of your own mistakes.

Six Feral cards arm it, and a permanent gauge shows exactly what detonating deals and what it costs you — so it is never a random punishment. Hold at eighteen and it goes off on its own. Every turn you wait makes the bomb bigger, the recoil worse and your hand deader. Set it off and every strain collapses back to its cap; you rebuild from half a colony.

The enemies watch what you are breeding, and they leave you a tell.

Nineteen of them, every attack telegraphed two turns ahead with a condition written underneath it. Meet the condition before you end your turn and the blow lands light. The check reads your colony at the moment you stop — so the forecast is never only "how much is this going to hurt," it is "what am I allowed to do this turn."

Every run runs on different physics.

You sign a Contract before you pick a single strain, and it rewrites the rules for the whole run — one restriction and one compensation, never just "harder this time." Drought crushes every cap but breeds you an extra creature. Bare Hands takes PRUNE away entirely. Monoculture gives you one strain instead of two, then makes it enormous. Choke doubles your overflow and lets you detonate twice as early.

The run ends on a sheet worth posting.

Win or die, you get a Herbarium specimen page: the strains you raised, the mutations that drifted into them, your peak population, your Blooms, the Contract you signed. Ten strains, three visible growth stages each, six heritable mutations — the colony you finish with is not one anybody else has had.

Features

  • 25–40 minute runs — five layers, and a boss announced on the very first screen: The Gardener, The Glasshouse or The Seedsman
  • Ten strains with three growth stages each, nineteen enemies, six heritable mutations that drift as your colony breeds
  • Six Contracts that change the run's physics; eleven post-battle nodes with five on offer every time
  • Five verbs and no bloat — HARVEST, SOW, BURN, PRUNE, DETONATE. You never do multiplication; every card previews its own result on hover
  • A screenshot-ready Herbarium sheet at the end of every run, win or lose

store_data.about_the_game:
THE MARKET IS A CASINO.

Wheel Street is a single-player financial roguelike deckbuilder played on a circular board. Read the week ahead, manipulate your assets, and assemble strategy-card combos that turn every market swing into increasingly absurd returns.

READ THE MARKET BEFORE IT MOVES

At the beginning of each week, the full five-day market outlook is revealed.

Land on an asset during an up day to cash in its current value. Hit it during a down day to double its value for the future. The market is not hiding anything from you—the challenge is arranging the board so that you are always in the right place at the right time.

Grow during the downturn. Cash out during the rise.

CONTROL THE BOARD

Each day, choose from three movement cards. Use one to move your pawn clockwise around the board, or spend your cards to reposition the assets themselves.

Move assets into empty spaces, merge matching sectors to combine their value, or swap different assets to reshape the board. Every position affects what you pass, where you land, and which effects will trigger.

Luck determines your options. You decide how to exploit them.

BUILD YOUR PORTFOLIO

Collect assets from technology, crypto, consumer goods, commodities, real estate, and banking.

Concentrate assets from the same sector to activate unique abilities, including dividends, sector rotation, leverage, futures, location bonuses, and compound interest.

Then add strategy cards that bend the rules of growth and settlement. Combine their conditions, control their trigger order, and create profitable chain reactions.

INVEST OR CASH OUT?

Your wallet is both your score and your spending power.

Investing in new assets can make your portfolio stronger, but every purchase also takes money away from your current weekly target. Decide when to reinvest, when to save, and when to push your luck for one more explosive payout.

Meet the target to advance, earn tokens, and visit the shop. Fall short, and the run is over.

EVERY RUN IS A NEW MARKET

Randomized starting assets, market patterns, card choices, and shop offerings turn every run into a new strategic puzzle.

Build around the opportunities you are given, discover unexpected combinations, and see how far your portfolio can climb before the market finally catches up with you.

  • Circular-board movement and asset positioning

  • Roguelike card and portfolio building

  • Fully visible market cycles

  • Six asset sectors with unique synergies

  • Strategy-card combos and chain reactions

  • Escalating weekly cash targets

  • Randomized runs with high replayability

No investment experience required. Terrible financial instincts welcome.

ONE TOWER. ENDLESS WAVES.

You get a single tower at the centre of the arena. Everything else is a decision about where the money goes.

Every wave you clear pays out immediately, and you spend it mid-run: damage, attack speed, crit chance, crit factor. Six weapon mounts fire at once — Tesla coil, mortar, beam laser, flak cannon, ricochet shredder, railgun — and each has its own upgrade lines. Run ends, cash converts, and the permanent side of the game opens up.

THE CONSTELLATION

453 passive nodes across six arms and six keystones. Points come from your progression level, not from clearing an arbitrary wave, so the tree is open from early on and keeps paying out for hundreds of runs. Sockets take jewels that rewrite what the nodes around them do.

BUILT AS A PREMIUM GAME

No ads. No timers. No energy bars. No currency sold for real money. You buy it once and the whole game is there.

WHAT'S IN IT

14 weapons, 6 simultaneous mounts, 10 sectors of escalating difficulty, a 453-node passive tree, jewel sockets and attunement, 64 achievements, offline earnings, and a workshop of permanent upgrades that raise where every future run begins.

store_data.about_the_game:
A failed energy experiment split the world into five unstable regions. Vikings now cross frozen oceans, mutants roam the ruins, machines guard an abandoned citadel, and creatures emerge from a place where the laws of physics no longer work.

You lead Aegis Division, a team sent to recover five Quantum Cores and rebuild the Eclipser Engine. To reach them, you will need to fight through 100 stages and defeat the boss controlling each region.

BUILD YOUR TEAM

Choose heroes from five classes: Tank, Sniper, RPG, Medic, and Tactician. Each class has a different role, so a strong team needs more than raw damage.

Place durable heroes on the front line, protect weaker units in the back, and adjust your formation to deal with different enemy teams. You can save formations and reuse them in later battles.

FIGHT YOUR WAY

Battles are turn-based. You can choose basic attacks, skills, ultimates, and targets manually. Skills consume energy, powerful abilities have cooldowns, and attack speed helps decide turn order.

If you would rather focus on building your team, turn on auto-battle. Your heroes will choose their actions and targets automatically, and you can return to manual control when needed.

UPGRADE AND EXPERIMENT

Heroes grow stronger as they level up and unlock new skills. Equip class-specific gear, upgrade abilities, collect buffs, and use shards to forge new heroes, gear, and upgrades.

Buffs can provide shields, healing, critical bonuses, armor penetration, reflection, camouflage, status effects, and other advantages. Different combinations may work better against different enemies.

EXPLORE FIVE REGIONS

The campaign takes you through the Frozen Dominion, Mutant Wastes, Infernal Depths, Cyborg Citadel, and Void Frontier. Each region has its own enemies and boss.

Recover every Quantum Core and decide what happens to the fractured world.

FEATURES

• Turn-based battles with optional auto-battle

• Five hero classes

• Manual control of attacks, skills, ultimates, and targets

• Front- and back-line formation building

• Hero levels and skill upgrades

• Gear, buffs, forging, and team progression

• 100 single-player campaign stages

• Five regions with different enemies and bosses

• English, Japanese, and Arabic interface support

Take Japan to the Top

Take charge of Japan's national volleyball team. Select and develop players, then lead your team into international competition.

Will you focus on winning now, or invest in developing the next generation?

Same alley, same night, never the same danger

You're trapped in a cramped, dimly lit alley that winds past old houses, rusted iron gates, and tangled power lines. There's only one way out — light all 10 candles.

store_data.about_the_game:
She was the only one who could read it. Now she's dead, and it's still running.

A rune-tape program runs the pressure ward that keeps the Drifted City aloft. It ran correctly for eleven years. Last night it killed the engineer who maintained it.

You have her listing. Her logs. Her stepper.

Find the instruction that did it.

You never write a line of code. You read one.

Faultfinder is a deduction game with a debugger for a magnifying glass. Every case opens as three panes: her annotated listing on the left, the machine's live state in the middle, and on the right what the city actually observed. A pressure reading that held at zero for nine seconds. A door that reported closed while it stood open.

Your tools are a debugger's, not a programmer's:

  • Step one instruction and watch exactly one thing change.

  • Break on a line, or on a condition: stop when PRESSURE drops below four.

  • Watch a register and read its whole history as a strip beside the tape.

  • Rewind. The entire trace is recorded. The scrub bar runs both ways.

  • Inject a different reading from the outside world and re-run it. Some faults only wake for one input in a thousand.

Then you commit. Name one line. Name one fault from a fixed vocabulary: off-by-one boundary, uninitialised register, wrong branch polarity, overwritten value, unit mismatch, missing bounds check. Then name the moment the harm was done. Get all three right and the report writes itself, one clause at a time.

Every case has exactly one answer. That is not a promise. It is a proof.

Faultfinder's cases aren't designed and playtested into fairness. They're machine-verified before they ship. Each one is built by taking a correct program, applying a single seeded fault, and then proving by exhaustive simulation across the whole input space that the faulty program fails, that reverting that one instruction fixes it, and that no other single change can.

If a case has a second defensible answer, the pipeline rejects it and you never see it. No designer ever adjudicates whether your reasoning was fair. The machine already did.

The program is a character document.

M. VOSK kept this ward for eleven years. She annotated her own tape in pencil, translating each rune for herself in her first year, because nobody had taught her either.

Her glosses thin as the cases go on. Her comments get terser. There is a line she commented out, years ago, with the note leave this.

You are the first person in eleven years to read her carefully. You are eleven years late.

For the specific pleasure almost no game has dramatised

If you have ever written software, you know the feeling of a bug collapsing into obviousness. The moment a mess becomes a sentence. Faultfinder makes that collapse the win condition and puts a body underneath it.

And if you haven't: you don't need to. Nothing here asks you to author anything. The blank page is the wall that keeps most players out of programming games, and this game does not have one. Her handwritten gloss sits beside every rune in the first case. Hover translates anything, always. No case is ever gated on remembering.

In the demo

  • Seven cases, 35 to 70 minutes, on one machine: the pressure ward on the city's underside

  • A fourteen-instruction rune-tape, taught by using it

  • Six classes of fault, each hiding in a different way

  • Full rewind, conditional breakpoints, register watches and input injection

  • Her story, told entirely in marginalia and log fragments

Wishlist Faultfinder to hear when the full ward opens.

A solo studio in Somerset. Built in Godot.

Paver: Tidy Up Together is a satisfying first-person organizing game where you sort and place pavers to rebuild a plaza. Work at your own pace, follow the correct patterns, unlock useful skills, and watch a chaotic area gradually transform into a perfectly restored plaza.

Game Modes

Play solo or together in online co-op.

  • Normal Mode: Progress normally and unlock new skills as you play.

  • Sandbox Mode: Jump straight in with all the skills unlocked. 

  • No-Skill Mode: Challenge yourself with all skills disabled and complete the layout manually.

Paver Layout Plan

The restoration of the old castle is nearly complete—but the grand plaza is still unfinished. During the renovation, all pavers are mixed across the ground. Fortunately, you have the original paver layout plan. Your task is to place 4,064 pavers in the correct places. There are pavers with different colors, and also different shapes like rectangle, square, octagon, trapezoid, H-shaped, triangle, hexagon, trihex, and radial.

Skills

  • Highlighting Paver Layout: Highlights the correct place for the topmost paver in your hand

  • Auto-Placement: Automatically places your pavers in the correct places

  • Auto-Collect: Automatically collects the same pavers as the topmost paver in your hand

store_data.about_the_game:
The Freshest Meat in Town

Dead & Delicious is a first-person co-op simulator about running a burger joint during a zombie outbreak. Out front, customers are waiting for their order. Out back, the horde is coming. You'll be doing both jobs at once, and you'll be doing them badly. That's the fun part.

Two Jobs, One Counter

Customers and zombies show up at the same time. Someone has to take the order. Someone has to hold the back door. Nobody has time for either. Balancing the register and the shotgun is the entire game, and it falls apart in the best possible way.

Fresh Cuts

Pistols, shotguns, katanas and other close-range tools are all on the menu. Zombies come apart where you hit them: shoot the head clean off, take a leg with a blade and watch it drag itself toward you anyway. Every kill is a physics-driven mess, and every mess is an ingredient.

From the Back Door to the Bun

Haul the pieces inside and load up the meat grinder. Crank the handle, pack the meat, and drop a fresh patty on the grill. Cook it right, stack the burger, hand it over. Simple work, if the shop weren't actively being overrun.

Upgrade the Joint

Spend what you earn on better gear and a better shop. Improve your equipment, expand your setup and make each shift a little less impossible than the last.

Ragdoll Everything

Nothing in this restaurant stands up straight. Your character wobbles as you run, zombies flop when they drop, and one well-aimed object from a teammate will put you on the floor mid-order. Physics is the co-chef, and it is not on your side.

1-4 Players, Online or Solo

Play alone or bring up to three friends online. There are no assigned roles, no classes and no forced jobs. Anyone can cook, anyone can shoot, and figuring out who does what is up to you.

Key Features

Co-op for 1-4 players - play solo or online with friends

Cook and fight at the same time - customers and zombies arrive together

Location-based dismemberment - heads, arms and legs come off where you hit

Firearms and melee - pistols, shotguns, katanas and more

Full meat pipeline - grind the pieces, form the patty, grill it, serve it

Shop and gear upgrades - spend your earnings to survive the next shift

Ragdoll physics everywhere - on the zombies, on the food, on you

Stylized first-person visuals - cartoony, colorful and deeply unserious

content_descriptors.notes:
Dead & Delicious contains frequent cartoon violence and gore in a stylized, non-realistic art style.

Players use firearms and melee weapons against zombies. Enemies can be dismembered, and heads, arms and legs can be severed and detached depending on where they are hit. This is accompanied by stylized blood effects and exaggerated ragdoll physics. Dismembered enemies may continue to move toward the player.

The core premise of the game involves processing the remains of zombies into food. Players carry body parts to a meat grinder, turn them into patties, cook them and serve them to customers who are unaware of what the food is made from. This is presented as dark comedy and is played entirely for humor.

The game does not contain sexual content, nudity, or depictions of self-harm. It does not contain the use of drugs or alcohol. Enemies are undead, not living human characters.

Those they loved.
Those they hated.
Those who were mere acquaintances.

The dead who stand trial in the Underworld must recount the life they have lived and defend themselves in their own words.

“I lived a virtuous life.”
“I had no other choice.”
“I am not guilty.”

The Velvet Bean has two faces

Your aunt Margot left you a cafe you visited exactly twice. Her lawyer smiled when he slid the keys across the desk, and the last line of her letter reads: "Ask Selene about the Ledger. When she trusts you."

By day the Velvet Bean is an ordinary third-wave coffee bar. On Friday and Saturday nights it becomes something else entirely — the place this city's femboy and futa regulars come to stop performing. The thing that built that second identity was Margot's Velvet Ledger, and the Ledger is missing.

You have forty-five days. Aurea, the chain empire across the block, holds an option on your lease that comes due on the last one. Keep the cafe standing and pay it, or hand Margot's life over to the woman who has been circling it since the funeral.

Six people worth staying open for

Selene, 34. Head barista, and the spine of the place. Dominant, dry, hides her warmth behind needling. She was Margot's right hand, and she does not intend to lose this cafe twice.

Lulu, 21. Pastry chef. Shy, sweet, happiest behind the oven. His family doesn't know who he is; here, he doesn't have to explain.

Coco, 23. Server. Loud, flirtatious, permanently attached to his phone and determined to make the cafe go viral. He's a completely different person once the camera is off.

Nova, 26. Night-shift barista and the door's quiet gatekeeper. Gothic, sparing with words. She used to be Aurea's star, and she is not ready to talk about why she left.

Roxy, 25. Weekend DJ and the architect of the cafe's night identity. Insolent, playful, allergic to rules. He never gives anyone a second night.

Valentina, 31. Aurea's owner. Elegant, arrogant, dangerously easy to look at. She is the reason you may lose everything. She is also the only other person who ever loved Margot.

Run the cafe, then close it and see who stays

Every day runs on the same rhythm and none of them play out the same way.

Morning. Set the menu, invest in decor, and put two people on shift. Money is made and spent here.

Day. Work the shift you staffed. Coffee Rush and Night Mixer are short, generous skill games; performance sets your takings and warms the people you worked beside.

Evening. Choose one person to spend your free hours with. This is where the routes move.

Night. Twice a week the second face comes out: masquerades, karaoke, latte-art duels, a neon picnic, and a Silent Night that belongs entirely to Nova.

The management layer is deliberately forgiving. This is a visual novel with a cafe attached, not a spreadsheet with a romance attached.

Three acts, forty-five days, eight endings

The Velvet Ledger returns one page at a time, and the last page rewrites everything you thought this fight was about. Six full romance routes run alongside it, each with its own crisis to survive — a video that spreads the way Coco never wanted, a secret of Nova's that detonates in the middle of a shift, the wall Roxy puts up the moment anything starts to feel permanent.

Save the cafe and the ending is yours to choose: any of the six character endings you qualified for, or the "Family" ending if what you built here was never about romance. Fail the Midnight Festival and you get the ending you earned instead.

A situation card appears on everyone's screen. You have 15 seconds to choose a video meme from your hand — the one that answers it best, or the one that's so wrong it's perfect.

- All chosen memes play back, one after another

- Everyone votes for the best answer, anonymously

Layer. Blend. Matching colors disappear.

Place colored pieces onto the board. Red, blue and yellow blend into purple, green and orange; all three together make black, and white lightens whatever it touches. Layer the same color again and that component cancels out and vanishes. Match every cell of the target pattern to clear the puzzle.

Exactly one solution — always

Every puzzle is generated backwards from a finished board, and its uniqueness is verified by an exhaustive count. You will never stumble onto an accidental second answer.

1000 puzzles, graded by depth — not by color count

Four tiers — Easy (4x4, three colors), Normal, Hard and Oni — with the piece count stepping up inside each tier. Adding more colors does not make a puzzle harder; only how many pieces stack on a single color does. That structure is the difficulty curve.

Only the good boards made the cut

Far more puzzles were generated than shipped, then ranked by "small color clumps, many distinct colors" and taken from the top. The selection exists for one reason: so that neighboring cells blend into many different colors.

Built to sit well in the hand

Play with mouse or keyboard. Each of the twelve actions takes up to two key bindings, and the wheel swaps pieces. The board is drawn like layered sheets of colored washi paper.

The mining colony has ore. The bugs have an appetite.

You have an orbital station, an irresponsible quantity of firepower and one simple order: keep the colony off the menu.

Build towers. Call strikes. Burn the sky. Survive swarms of billions of bugs in a tower defense built around huge battles, persistent progression and increasingly excessive solutions.

The only good bug is a dead bug.

Would you like to know more?

BILLIONS OF BUGS. GIVE OR TAKE.

Workers flood the battlefield. Armored grunts smash through kill zones. Darts skitter past your defenses. Spitters attack from range. Skyrays ignore your carefully prepared ground defenses. Colossi refuse to die. Queens arrive to ruin everybody’s day. Kings mean it's over.

Fortunately, you have guns.

Lots of guns.

Build during the calm, then watch the swarm pour across the map. Reinforce chokepoints, replace destroyed positions and adapt before the next wave turns your perfect defense into a cautionary tale.

DEFEND THE COLONY TOGETHER

Play solo or bring up to three fellow citizens into 2–4 player Steam co-op.

Host a friends-only or public lobby, invite through Steam or jump into Quick Match. Fight together across campaign battlefields, custom maps and subscribed Workshop creations.

Share the battlefield. Split the spoils. Bring your own unlocks. Try not to blame each other when the eastern wall collapses.

A FULL CAMPAIGN

Fight through 26 handcrafted battlefields, each with its own paths, chokepoints and tactical problems.

Every map is a new defensive puzzle. Seal the outpost, unlock the next deployment and push deeper into a campaign where the bugs grow meaner and your arsenal grows much, much louder.

INFINITE PROCEDURAL DEPLOYMENTS

Enter SURGE for a newly generated battlefield every run.

Random layouts, changing nest positions and unpredictable geometry force you to build a fresh defense instead of repeating the same winning pattern forever.

The war continues for as long as you do.

BUILD YOUR OWN BATTLEFIELDS

Open the built-in map editor and paint the warzone yourself.

Create walls, carve paths, position nests, test routes and build anything from a carefully balanced challenge to an absolute tactical nightmare.

Save your creations locally, publish them to Steam Workshop and subscribe to maps built by other players. Then defend them alone or bring them into co-op.

EIGHT TOWERS. SEVEN WAYS TO RUIN A BUG’S DAY.

Build an arsenal of:

  • Gatling turrets

  • Acid sprayers

  • Plasma cannons

  • Cryo towers

  • Sniper emplacements

  • Mortars

  • Tesla towers

  • Flame turrets

Then call in the heavy equipment:

  • Orbital strikes

  • Napalm

  • Cryo-EMP

  • Acid rain

  • Ion storms

  • Gravity wells

  • Bait drops

When the chokepoint fails, remember: you still have the high ground.

The very, very high ground.

A MASSIVE UPGRADE TREE

Every deployment strengthens the next.

Harvest ore, earn gems and advance through 165 persistent upgrades covering towers, orbital powers and prestige bonuses.

Unlock new weapons. Specialize each tower through multiple upgrade paths. Improve your starting economy, reinforce your defenses and turn yesterday’s desperate last stand into tomorrow’s routine pest control.

Lost the run?

The bugs may have won the battle, but they still funded your upgrade budget.

KNOW YOUR ENEMY

The Bug Index tracks seven enemy species, their armor, their behavior and the towers best suited to killing them.

Learn what flies, what spits, what charges and what simply refuses to stop moving.

Then build the correct counter.

Or use more napalm.

Both are valid strategic doctrines.

AROUND 60 HOURS OF MUSIC

Defend humanity to a colossal 986-track soundtrack spanning roughly 60 hours.

Skip tracks, control the volume or let the soundtrack carry you through a campaign, a co-op deployment or one more procedural run that definitely will not last until sunrise.

store_data.about_the_game:
Zombie Mystery: 100 Hidden Cats Rescue the Lost Cats of the Zombie Apocalypse!

As the world is shaken by a zombie outbreak, hundreds of cats are hiding in abandoned streets just to survive. Every scene awaits you in a deserted yet richly detailed environment… but beware, these frightened cats are cleverly hidden and won't give themselves away easily!

Game Features:

  • Race Against Time — The game is entirely time-based. The faster you find the cats, the higher you climb. Players who finish in the shortest time claim their spot on the global leaderboard.

  • Hint System — If a cat proves too tricky, press the hint button to reveal its location. Just remember, every hint used adds extra time to your final score.

  • Wrong Click Penalty — Clicking the wrong spot adds a time penalty, and consecutive wrong clicks stack the penalty even higher. Precision matters just as much as speed.

  • Achievements — Unlock achievements as you progress and crown your journey. Speed, precision, and exploration await you.

Are you ready? Find the lost cats, rescue them, manage your time, and write your name into the global leaderboard!
